Approximation Theory for Lipschitz Continuous Transformers

Takashi Furuya Affiliation: Faculty of Life and Medical Sciences, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Doshisha University, RIKEN AIP Correspondence to: takashi.furuya0101@gmail.com    Davide Murari Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics, University of Cambridge Correspondence to: dm2011@cam.ac.uk    Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics, University of Cambridge Correspondence to: cbs31@cam.ac.uk
Abstract

Stability and robustness are critical for deploying Transformers in safety-sensitive settings. A principled way to enforce such behavior is to constrain the model’s Lipschitz constant. However, approximation-theoretic guarantees for architectures that explicitly preserve Lipschitz continuity have yet to be established. In this work, we bridge this gap by introducing a class of gradient-descent-type in-context Transformers that are Lipschitz-continuous by construction. We realize both MLP and attention blocks as explicit Euler steps of negative gradient flows, ensuring inherent stability without sacrificing expressivity. We prove a universal approximation theorem for this class within a Lipschitz-constrained function space. Crucially, our analysis adopts a measure-theoretic formalism, interpreting Transformers as operators on probability measures, to yield approximation guarantees independent of token count. These results provide a rigorous theoretical foundation for the design of robust, Lipschitz continuous Transformer architectures.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Transformers are at the forefront of contemporary machine learning, but are susceptible to adversarial examples (Gupta & Verma, 2023; Xu et al., 2023), and can be unstable to train (Liu et al., 2020; Davis et al., 2021; Qi et al., 2023). A mathematically sound remedy against these issues is to control the Lipschitz constant of the input-to-output map they realize.

Getting reliable Lipschitz control is structurally challenging in Transformers. Standard self-attention involves unbounded dot products of linear projections, rendering it non-globally Lipschitz continuous (Kim et al., 2021). These issues are further exacerbated by the residual connections, which do not yield tight bounds on their Lipschitz constants (Xu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023). Since computing a map’s Lipschitz constant is NP-hard (Virmaux & Scaman, 2018), controlling the Lipschitz constant of Transformers is typically achieved by modifying and constraining a new architecture. Existing methods typically rely on spectral regularization, modifications to the self-attention layer, and the weighting of residual layers.

Among the various Lipschitz constraints, the 11-Lipschitz case is particularly natural (Sherry et al., 2024; Murari et al., 2025; Prach et al., 2023; Béthune et al., 2022; Hasannasab et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2023; Anil et al., 2019; Anonymous, 2026). First, it is sometimes a necessary modeling requirement: 11-Lipschitz function classes arise as the admissible critics to approximate the Wasserstein-11 distance (Arjovsky et al., 2017), and being 11-Lipschitz is the baseline condition needed to obtain contraction maps in fixed-point iterations and stability analyzes. Second, even when one ultimately cares about an LL-Lipschitz model, restricting the focus to 11-Lipschitz maps is largely without loss of generality, since any LL-Lipschitz map can be written as a simple rescaling of a 11-Lipschitz map (Béthune et al., 2022). This makes 1-Lipschitzness a convenient normalization since it fixes a canonical scale for sensitivity while retaining the essential approximation questions within a standardized function class.

Transformers can be viewed as in-context maps in the sense that they take as input both a context and a distinguished query (or query token) and output a prediction that depends on both. Requiring the resulting map to be 11-Lipschitz with respect to the query for each fixed context ensures nonexpansiveness with respect to the query, which is useful, for instance, in learned fixed-point schemes that require convergence guarantees. This parallels the context-free setting; see (Hasannasab et al., 2019; Sherry et al., 2024). In the in-context case, however, varying the context changes the induced query-to-output transformation, effectively yielding a family of maps parameterized by the context. We therefore also require Lipschitz continuity with respect to the context for each fixed query, to ensure stability and robustness under small perturbations of the context. In this work, we model the context as a probability measure and control its effect via Lipschitz continuity with respect to the Wasserstein-11 distance.

We introduce a Transformer architecture that is provably 1-Lipschitz with respect to the query for any fixed context, and admits a finite Lipschitz constant as a function of the context. The 11-Lipschitz bound is independent of the context length, and our layer is defined in the more general setting where the context is a measure. Moreover, we theoretically analyze the approximation capabilities of these models, proving universal approximation for the class of 1-Lipschitz in-context maps on compact domains. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first theoretical investigation of the approximation properties of 11-Lipschitz in-context maps.

1.1 Related work

Lipschitz-constrained neural networks

Lipschitz control has been pursued as a principled mechanism for stability, robustness, and regularization of neural networks. Such a control on the Lipschitz constant is usually achieved by constraining the operator norms of linear layers during training (Miyato et al., 2018; Gouk et al., 2021; Bungert et al., 2021; Trockman & Kolter, 2021), and encoding non-expansiveness structurally through architectural design (Cisse et al., 2017; Sherry et al., 2024; Meunier et al., 2021). Especially when new architectural choices are made, some study of the network expressivity is necessary. A growing body of papers is exploring the theoretical approximation properties of Lipschitz-constrained networks. (Anil et al., 2019; Neumayer et al., 2023) study 11-Lipschitz feedforward networks, and (Murari et al., 2025) 11-Lipschitz ResNets. Our work builds on results from Section 3 of (Murari et al., 2025), but significantly extends their theory to accommodate the context measure, which plays a crucial role in Transformers.

Lipschitz-constrained Transformers.

Enforcing Lipschitz guarantees in Transformers is challenging because key components are not globally Lipschitz under standard formulations; in particular, dot-product self-attention is not globally Lipschitz on unbounded domains (Kim et al., 2021). Prior work pursues Lipschitz control through architectural changes, including replacing dot-product attention with Lipschitz-controlled variants (Kim et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2023), modifying normalization (e.g., CenterNorm in LipsFormer) (Qi et al., 2023), and reweighting residual branches to prevent depth-wise growth of sensitivity (Qi et al., 2023; Newhouse et al., 2025). A particular mention needs to be made for the recent paper (Anonymous, 2026), where the authors construct a 11-Lipschitz self-attention layer starting from convex gradient flows, similarly to how we approach the layer design. Our paper distinguishes from (Anonymous, 2026) in that we study the approximation properties of our newly proposed models, and rely on explicit layers rather than proximal maps to define the self-attention layer. Complementary contributions sharpen component-wise analysis, such as tight Lipschitz constants for softmax (Nair, 2026), and develop training-time norm-enforcement methods that aim to retain accuracy while providing explicit bounds (Newhouse et al., 2025). A substantial body of work, especially in vision, leverages Lipschitz control for certified robustness of transformer models (Xu et al., 2023; Menon et al., 2025; Gupta & Verma, 2023).

Approximation theory of Transformers

The expressivity of Transformer architectures has been studied extensively. The foundational work of (Yun et al., 2020) established that Transformers with sufficient depth and width are universal approximators of continuous permutation-equivariant sequence-to-sequence functions on compact domains. Subsequent research has refined these guarantees, investigating the specific roles of positional encodings and attention heads in recognizing formal languages (Bhattamishra et al., 2020). From a computational perspective, (Pérez et al., 2021) demonstrated that Transformers with hard attention are Turing complete under arbitrary precision assumptions.

More recently, the theoretical analysis has shifted toward the in-context learning setting. (Akyürek et al., 2023) and (von Oswald et al., 2023) show that Transformers can implement explicit learning algorithms, including gradient-descent-type updates, within their forward pass. Crucially, (Furuya et al., 2025) recently advanced this analysis by adopting a measure-theoretic formalism, proving that Transformers are universal in-context learners with approximation rates independent of the token count.

1.2 Contributions

We summarize our main contributions as follows.

  • •

    Lipschitz continuous in-context Transformers. We introduce a new class of in-context Transformer architectures in which both the MLP and attention blocks are interpreted as explicit Euler steps of negative gradient flows. This design yields gradient-descent-type updates and allows for enforcing Lipschitz continuity of the resulting input-to-output map. Such a map is 11-Lipschitz with respect to the input query.

  • •

    Universal approximation under explicit Lipschitz control. We prove a universal approximation theorem for the proposed Lipschitz continuous in-context Transformers. To the best of our knowledge, this provides the first approximation-theoretic guarantee for Transformer architectures that explicitly preserve Lipschitz continuity. Existing works primarily focus on analyzing or estimating Lipschitz properties rather than establishing approximation results.

  • •

    Measure-theoretic in-context formulation with token-independent guarantees. We cast in-context Transformers as operators acting on probability measures, and derive approximation guarantees that are independent of the number of tokens. The primary technical tool is a modification of the Restricted Stone–Weierstrass Theorem tailored to the measure-theoretic in-context setting. Since the Restricted Stone–Weierstrass framework is inherently constructive, our theoretical analysis also provides insights that are relevant for practical architectural design.

2.2 Lipschitz MLP layer

We define the gradient-decent-type MLP mapping Fξ:ℝd→ℝdF_{\xi}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} by

Fξ​(x):=x−τ​W⊤​σ​(W​x+b)F_{\xi}(x):=x-\tau W^{\top}\sigma(Wx+b) (1)

where the learnable parameter is denoted by ξ=(W,b,τ)\xi=(W,b,\tau), for a choice of W∈ℝk×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}, b∈ℝkb\in\mathbb{R}^{k}, and τ≥0\tau\geq 0. The map FξF_{\xi} can be interpreted as a single explicit Euler step of size τ\tau for the negative gradient flow equation x˙=−∇g​(x)\dot{x}=-\nabla g(x) where g⁡(x):=1⊤​γ​(W​x+b)g(x):=1^{\top}\gamma(Wx+b), γ′=σ\gamma^{\prime}=\sigma and 1∈ℝk1\in\mathbb{R}^{k} is a vector of ones. ResNets with layers FξF_{\xi} have been used in (Meunier et al., 2021; Prach et al., 2023; Sherry et al., 2024) to improve the robustness to adversarial attacks, and in (Sherry et al., 2024) to approximate the proximal operator and develop a provably convergent Plug-and-Play algorithm for inverse problems. In what follows, we fix σ=ReLU\sigma=\mathrm{ReLU}. We recall the following lemma.

Lemma 1.

(Sherry et al., 2024, Theorem 2.3 and Lemma 2.5) Assuming that τ∈[0,2/‖W‖22]\tau\in[0,2/\|W\|_{2}^{2}], then the map Fξ:(ℝd,∥⋅∥2)→(ℝd,∥⋅∥2)F_{\xi}:(\mathbb{R}^{d},\|\cdot\|_{2})\to(\mathbb{R}^{d},\|\cdot\|_{2}) defined in (1) with σ=ReLU\sigma=\mathrm{ReLU} is 1-Lipschitz continuous.

ResNets with these types of layers were shown to be universal for the set of scalar 11-Lipschitz functions in (Murari et al., 2025) and to provide a good trade-off between robustness and computational cost compared with alternatives in (Prach et al., 2023). The networks we consider in this paper rely on FξF_{\xi} as the context-free maps. We then build on the construction behind their expression to define the contextual mapping introduced in the next section.

4 Approximation result

4.1 Main result

Let C>0C>0 and d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, and let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact set. We define the input space as

𝒳:=𝒫⁡(Ω)×Ω.\mathcal{X}:=\mathcal{P}(\Omega)\times\Omega.

We denote by 𝒞1,C​(𝒳,ℝ)\mathcal{C}_{1,C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}) the class of scalar target mappings

𝒞1,C\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{1,C} (𝒳,ℝ):={F:𝒳→ℝ:\displaystyle(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}):=\Big\{F:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}:
F(μ,⋅):(Ω,∥⋅∥2)→(ℝ,|⋅|) is 1-Lipschitz\displaystyle F(\mu,\cdot):(\Omega,\|\cdot\|_{2})\to(\mathbb{R},|\cdot|)\text{ is $1$-Lipschitz}
F(⋅,x):(𝒫(Ω),W1)→(ℝ,|⋅|) is C-Lipschitz}.\displaystyle F(\cdot,x):(\mathcal{P}(\Omega),W_{1})\to(\mathbb{R},|\cdot|)\text{ is $C$-Lipschitz}\Big\}.
Remark 7.

We remark that all the functions in 𝒞1,C​(𝒳,ℝ)\mathcal{C}_{1,C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}) are Lipschitz continuous in the product metric since for every pair (μ,x),(ν,y)∈𝒳(\mu,x),(\nu,y)\in\mathcal{X} it holds

|F⁡(ν,y)−F⁡(μ,x)|\displaystyle|F(\nu,y)-F(\mu,x)|
=|F⁡(ν,y)−F⁡(ν,x)+F⁡(ν,x)−F⁡(μ,x)|\displaystyle=|F(\nu,y)-F(\nu,x)+F(\nu,x)-F(\mu,x)|
≤‖y−x‖2+C​W1​(μ,ν)\displaystyle\leq\|y-x\|_{2}+CW_{1}(\mu,\nu)
≤max⁡{1,C}​d​((x,μ),(y,ν)),\displaystyle\leq\max\{1,C\}d((x,\mu),(y,\nu)),

where dd is the product metric defined over 𝒳=𝒫⁡(Ω)×Ω\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{P}(\Omega)\times\Omega, i.e. d⁡((x,μ),(y,μ))=‖y−x‖2+W1​(μ,ν)d((x,\mu),(y,\mu))=\|y-x\|_{2}+W_{1}(\mu,\nu).

We define the class of scalar Lipschitz deep Transformers with lifting and projection:

𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ):=𝒞1,C​(𝒳,ℝ)∩𝒦⁡(𝒳,ℝ)\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}):=\mathcal{C}_{1,C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R})\cap\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R})

where

𝒦⁡(𝒳,ℝ)\displaystyle\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}) :={v⊤∘T∘Q¯:𝒳→ℝ:\displaystyle:=\Big\{v^{\top}\circ T\circ\bar{Q}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}\,:
Q∈𝒬d,h,Ω,Ω1,v∈ℝh,T∈𝒯h,Ω1,h∈ℕ,\displaystyle Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{d,h,\Omega,\Omega_{1}},v\in\mathbb{R}^{h},\,T\in\mathcal{T}_{h,\Omega_{1}},\,h\in\mathbb{N},
Ω1⊂ℝh compact with Q(Ω)⊂Ω1}.\displaystyle\Omega_{1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{h}\text{ compact with }Q(\Omega)\subset\Omega_{1}\Big\}.

Here, v⊤v^{\top} denotes the linear projection onto a one-dimensional output. The map QQ is a lifting mapping, defined as an affine embedding

𝒬d,h,Ω,Ω1:={Q:ℝd→ℝh:Q(x)=Ax+b,\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{d,h,\Omega,\Omega_{1}}:=\{Q:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{h}\,:\,Q(x)=Ax+b,
A∈ℝh×d,b∈ℝh,Q(Ω)⊂Ω1}.\displaystyle A\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times d},\,b\in\mathbb{R}^{h},\,Q(\Omega)\subset\Omega_{1}\}.

The map Q¯\bar{Q} is defined by

Q¯:𝒫⁡(ℝd)×ℝd→𝒫⁡(ℝh)×ℝh\displaystyle\bar{Q}:\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{h})\times\mathbb{R}^{h}
Q¯​(μ,x):=(Q♯​μ,Q⁡(x)), (context-free mapping).\displaystyle\bar{Q}(\mu,x):=(Q_{\sharp}\mu,Q(x)),\text{ (context-free mapping)}.

Note that, in general, the map v⊤∘T∘Q¯∈𝒦⁡(𝒳,ℝ)v^{\top}\circ T\circ\bar{Q}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}) does not necessarily belong to 𝒞1,C​(𝒳,ℝ)\mathcal{C}_{1,C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}), since we do not impose ‖v‖2≤1\|v\|_{2}\leq 1 and ‖Q‖2≤1\|Q\|_{2}\leq 1. This is why 𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ)\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}) is defined by intersecting 𝒦⁡(𝒳,ℝ)\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}) with 𝒞1,C​(𝒳,ℝ)\mathcal{C}_{1,C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}), so we can ensure a controlled Lipschitz constant. We remark that this technique of intersecting with the target set is common in theoretical studies, see, for example, (Murari et al., 2025; Eckstein, 2020). Moreover, for any T∈𝒯h,Ω1T\in\mathcal{T}_{h,\Omega_{1}}, the map TT is always 11-Lipschitz with respect to the query variable and C2C_{2}-Lipschitz with respect to the context measure, for worst-case Lipschitz constant C2>0C_{2}>0 given by Lemma 6.

We now ask whether a deep Transformer that is 11-Lipschitz in the query variable and CC-Lipschitz in the context variable, for an arbitrary prescribed constant C>0C>0, can approximate any continuous in-context map with the same Lipschitz constraints. The main result of this paper answers this question in the affirmative.

Theorem 8.

Let C>0C>0 and d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}. Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact set. Then, for any ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) and any Λ∗∈𝒞1,C​(𝒳,ℝ)\Lambda^{*}\in\mathcal{C}_{1,C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}), there is Λ∈𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ)\Lambda\in\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}) such that

sup(μ,x)∈𝒳|Λ⁡(μ,x)−Λ∗​(μ,x)|≤ε.\sup_{(\mu,x)\in\mathcal{X}}|\Lambda(\mu,x)-\Lambda^{*}(\mu,x)|\leq\varepsilon.

This is, to the best of our knowledge, the first theoretical approximation result for Transformer architectures that preserve Lipschitz continuity. More precisely, we show that gradient-descent-type in-context Transformers can approximate arbitrary Lipschitz continuous in-context maps.

Our result can be viewed as a generalization of (Murari et al., 2025, Theorem 3.1) to in-context mappings by incorporating an additional argument corresponding to the token measure. This extension is highly nontrivial: the proof requires a variant of the Restricted Stone–Weierstrass theorem (Lemma 9) adapted to functions of two variables, including probability measures.

Key technical ingredients used to verify the hypotheses of this theorem include concatenation arguments (Lemma 11) and Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality-based lower-bounds (Lemma 13). These tools are specific to the measure-theoretic in-context setting and are fundamentally different from the Euclidean-space arguments employed in (Murari et al., 2025).

4.2 Proof of Theorem 8

The proof of Theorem 8 is based on a variant of the Restricted Stone–Weierstrass theorem, adapted to Lipschitz functions of two variables. We first state the abstract approximation result.

Lemma 9 (Variant of the Restricted Stone–Weierstrass theorem).

Let (U,dU)(U,d_{U}) and (X,dX)(X,d_{X}) be compact metric spaces with at least two points, and let C>0C>0. We denote by 𝒞1,C​(U×X,ℝ)\mathcal{C}_{1,C}(U\times X,\mathbb{R}) the space of all functions f:U×X→ℝf:U\times X\to\mathbb{R} such that x↦f⁡(u,x)x\mapsto f(u,x) is 11-Lipschitz continuous for every u∈Uu\in U, and u↦f⁡(u,x)u\mapsto f(u,x) is CC-Lipschitz continuous for every x∈Xx\in X.

Let L⊂𝒞1,C​(U×X,ℝ)L\subset\mathcal{C}_{1,C}(U\times X,\mathbb{R}). Assume that:

  • (A)

    LL is a lattice, i.e., for any Λ,Λ′∈L\Lambda,\Lambda^{\prime}\in L, it holds that

    max⁡{Λ,Λ′}∈L,min⁡{Λ,Λ′}∈L.\max\{\Lambda,\Lambda^{\prime}\}\in L,\quad\min\{\Lambda,\Lambda^{\prime}\}\in L.
  • (B)

    LL separates points in the following Lipschitz sense: for any two distinct points (u,x),(v,y)∈U×X(u,x),(v,y)\in U\times X and any a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R} satisfying

    |a−b|<C​dU​(u,v)+dX​(x,y),|a-b|<C\,d_{U}(u,v)+d_{X}(x,y),

    there exists f∈Lf\in L such that

    f⁡(u,x)=a,f⁡(v,y)=b.f(u,x)=a,\quad f(v,y)=b.

Then LL is dense in 𝒞1,C​(U×X,ℝ)\mathcal{C}_{1,C}(U\times X,\mathbb{R}) with respect to the uniform norm.

See Appendix B for the proof.

Lemma 9 is a modification of the Restricted Stone–Weierstrass theorem given by (Anil et al., 2019, Lemma 1), extended to functions of two arguments and formulated with a strict separation condition. A key feature in the proof of the Restricted Stone–Weierstrass theorem is its practical nature. Rather than solely providing an existence density result, it yields an approximation based on the lattice structure generated by minimax compositions of elementary building blocks. Condition (A) guarantees closure under these lattice operations, while condition (B) ensures the existence of elementary building blocks.

The core of the proof of Theorem 8 is therefore to verify conditions (A) and (B) for the class 𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ)\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}) of gradient-descent-type in-context Transformers.

Condition (A)

We begin by verifying the lattice property.

Lemma 10.

The set 𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ)\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}) is a lattice, i.e., for any Λ,Λ′∈𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ)\Lambda,\Lambda^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}), it holds that

max⁡{Λ,Λ′}∈𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ),min⁡{Λ,Λ′}∈𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ).\max\{\Lambda,\Lambda^{\prime}\}\in\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}),\quad\min\{\Lambda,\Lambda^{\prime}\}\in\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}).

See Appendix C for the detailed proof.

The key idea is to show that the concatenation of two networks Λ\Lambda and Λ′\Lambda^{\prime} can be represented within the same architectural class, by composing MLPs and attention layers in parallel. More precisely, we observe that

(Λ⁡(μ,x)Λ′​(μ,x))=(v⊤00v′⁣⊤)∘(FξLFξL′)∘(ΓθL​(μL)ΓθL′​(μL′))∘⋯\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda(\mu,x)\\ \Lambda^{\prime}(\mu,x)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}v^{\top}&0\\ 0&v^{\prime\top}\end{pmatrix}\circ\begin{pmatrix}F_{\xi_{L}}\\ F_{\xi^{\prime}_{L}}\end{pmatrix}\circ\begin{pmatrix}\Gamma_{\theta_{L}}(\mu_{L})\\ \Gamma_{\theta^{\prime}_{L}}(\mu^{\prime}_{L})\end{pmatrix}\circ\cdots
∘(Fξ1Fξ1′)∘(Γθ1​(μ1)Γθ1′​(μ1′))∘(QQ′)⁡(x),\displaystyle\qquad\circ\begin{pmatrix}F_{\xi_{1}}\\ F_{\xi^{\prime}_{1}}\end{pmatrix}\circ\begin{pmatrix}\Gamma_{\theta_{1}}(\mu_{1})\\ \Gamma_{\theta^{\prime}_{1}}(\mu^{\prime}_{1})\end{pmatrix}\circ\begin{pmatrix}Q\\ Q^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}(x),

where Γθℓ∈𝒱d,Ωℓ,Ω~ℓ\Gamma_{\theta_{\ell}}\in\mathcal{V}_{d,\Omega_{\ell},\tilde{\Omega}_{\ell}}, Γθℓ′∈𝒱d,Ωℓ′,Ω~ℓ′\Gamma_{\theta^{\prime}_{\ell}}\in\mathcal{V}_{d,\Omega^{\prime}_{\ell},\tilde{\Omega}^{\prime}_{\ell}}, Fξℓ∈ℰd′,Ω~ℓ,Ωℓ+1F_{\xi_{\ell}}\in\mathcal{E}_{d^{\prime},\tilde{\Omega}_{\ell},\Omega_{\ell+1}}, and Fξℓ′∈ℰd′,Ω~ℓ′,Ωℓ+1′F_{\xi^{\prime}_{\ell}}\in\mathcal{E}_{d^{\prime},\tilde{\Omega}^{\prime}_{\ell},\Omega^{\prime}_{\ell+1}}. Using the argument of (Murari et al., 2025, Lemma 3.2), we can merge the parallel MLP layers, i.e.,

(FξℓFξℓ′)=Fξℓ′′\begin{pmatrix}F_{\xi_{\ell}}\\ F_{\xi^{\prime}_{\ell}}\end{pmatrix}=F_{\xi^{\prime\prime}_{\ell}}

for some Fξℓ′′∈ℰd+d′,Ω~ℓ×Ω~ℓ′,Ωℓ+1×Ωℓ+1′F_{\xi^{\prime\prime}_{\ell}}\in\mathcal{E}_{d+d^{\prime},\,\tilde{\Omega}_{\ell}\times\tilde{\Omega}^{\prime}_{\ell},\,\Omega_{\ell+1}\times\Omega^{\prime}_{\ell+1}}.

The technical difficulty in the proof of Lemma 10 is to show that an analogous concatenation is possible for attention layers. In general, this cannot be achieved by a single attention layer. Instead, we represent the parallel of two attention layers as a composition of two attention layers. More precisely, we prove the following lemma.

Lemma 11.

Let Γθ∈𝒱h,Ω,Ω~\Gamma_{\theta}\in\mathcal{V}_{h,\Omega,\tilde{\Omega}} and Γθ′∈𝒱h′,Ω′,Ω~′\Gamma_{\theta^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{V}_{h^{\prime},\Omega^{\prime},\tilde{\Omega}^{\prime}}. Then there exist Γθ1′′∈𝒱h+h′,Ω×Ω′,Ω~×Ω′\Gamma_{\theta^{\prime\prime}_{1}}\in\mathcal{V}_{h+h^{\prime},\,\Omega\times\Omega^{\prime},\,\tilde{\Omega}\times\Omega^{\prime}} and Γθ2′′∈𝒱h+h′,Ω~×Ω′,Ω~×Ω~′\Gamma_{\theta^{\prime\prime}_{2}}\in\mathcal{V}_{h+h^{\prime},\,\tilde{\Omega}\times\Omega^{\prime},\,\tilde{\Omega}\times\tilde{\Omega}^{\prime}} such that, for (μ,x)∈𝒫⁡(Ω)×Ω(\mu,x)\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega)\times\Omega, and (μ′,x′)∈𝒫⁡(Ω′)×Ω′(\mu^{\prime},x^{\prime})\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega^{\prime})\times\Omega^{\prime}, and γ∈Π⁡(μ,μ′)\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\mu^{\prime}), where Π⁡(μ,μ′)\Pi(\mu,\mu^{\prime}) denotes the set of all couplings of μ\mu and μ′\mu^{\prime}, we have

(Γθ​(μ,x)Γθ′​(μ′,x′))=π2∘Γ¯θ2′′∘Γ¯θ1′′​(γ,(xx′)).\begin{pmatrix}\Gamma_{\theta}(\mu,x)\\ \Gamma_{\theta^{\prime}}(\mu^{\prime},x^{\prime})\end{pmatrix}=\pi_{2}\circ\bar{\Gamma}_{\theta^{\prime\prime}_{2}}\circ\bar{\Gamma}_{\theta^{\prime\prime}_{1}}\Bigl(\gamma,\begin{pmatrix}x\\ x^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}\Bigr).

Here, π2\pi_{2} denotes the projection onto the query variable, and should not be confused with the projection onto the second component of a Cartesian product. Note that ReLU MLPs can represent the identity map, so the constructions in Lemma 11 can be realized by the alternating composition of context-free and in-context maps. See Appendix D for the proof.

Condition (B)

We next verify the separation property.

Lemma 12.

Let (μ,x),(μ′,x′)∈𝒳(\mu,x),(\mu^{\prime},x^{\prime})\in\mathcal{X} with (μ,x)≠(μ′,x′)(\mu,x)\neq(\mu^{\prime},x^{\prime}), and let a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R} with a≠ba\neq b, satisfy

|a−b|<‖x−x′‖2+C​W1​(μ,μ′).|a-b|<\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{2}+C\,W_{1}(\mu,\mu^{\prime}).

Then there exists Λ∈𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ)\Lambda\in\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}) such that

Λ⁡(μ,x)=a,Λ⁡(μ′,x′)=b.\Lambda(\mu,x)=a,\qquad\Lambda(\mu^{\prime},x^{\prime})=b.

See Appendix E for the detailed proof.

The proof of Lemma 12 relies on the following lower-bound result.

Lemma 13.

Let (μ,x),(μ′,x′)∈𝒳(\mu,x),(\mu^{\prime},x^{\prime})\in\mathcal{X}. Then for any ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), there exists Λ∈𝒢C​(𝒳)\Lambda\in\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X}) such that

C⁡(W1​(μ,μ′)−ε)≤Λ⁡(μ,x)−Λ⁡(μ′,x′).C\bigl(W_{1}(\mu,\mu^{\prime})-\varepsilon\bigr)\leq\Lambda(\mu,x)-\Lambda(\mu^{\prime},x^{\prime}).

We briefly outline the main idea of the proof. Let

ℱ:={φ:Ω→ℝ|Lip(φ)≤1,φ(x0)=0},\mathcal{F}:=\bigl\{\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\;\big|\;\mathrm{Lip}(\varphi)\leq 1,\ \varphi(x_{0})=0\bigr\},

for some fixed x0∈Ωx_{0}\in\Omega. By the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem, ℱ\mathcal{F} is compact. Since the map φ↦∫φ​d​(μ−μ′)\varphi\mapsto\int\varphi\,d(\mu-\mu^{\prime}) is continuous, there exists φ0∈ℱ\varphi_{0}\in\mathcal{F} such that

W1​(μ,μ′)=supφ∈ℱ∫φ​d​(μ−μ′)=∫φ0​d​(μ−μ′).W_{1}(\mu,\mu^{\prime})=\sup_{\varphi\in\mathcal{F}}\int\varphi\,d(\mu-\mu^{\prime})=\int\varphi_{0}\,d(\mu-\mu^{\prime}).

By (Murari et al., 2025, Theorem 3.1), there exist a compact set Ω1⊂ℝh\Omega_{1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{h}, Q∈𝒬d,h,Ω,Ω1Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{d,h,\Omega,\Omega_{1}}, v∈ℝhv\in\mathbb{R}^{h}, and a 11-Lipschitz map F:ℝh→ℝhF:\mathbb{R}^{h}\to\mathbb{R}^{h} given as a composition of gradient-decent-type MLPs such that

supz∈Ω|φ0​(z)−v⊤∘F∘Q⁡(z)|≤ε/2.\sup_{z\in\Omega}\bigl|\varphi_{0}(z)-v^{\top}\circ F\circ Q(z)\bigr|\leq\varepsilon/2.

This implies

W1​(μ,μ′)\displaystyle W_{1}(\mu,\mu^{\prime}) =∫φ0​d​(μ−μ′)\displaystyle=\int\varphi_{0}\,d(\mu-\mu^{\prime})
≤∫v⊤∘F∘Q​d​(μ−μ′)+ε.\displaystyle\leq\int v^{\top}\circ F\circ Q\,d(\mu-\mu^{\prime})+\varepsilon.

Finally, the term ∫v⊤∘F∘Q​d​(μ−μ′)\int v^{\top}\circ F\circ Q\,d(\mu-\mu^{\prime}) can be written as

Λ⁡(μ,x)−Λ⁡(μ′,x′)\Lambda(\mu,x)-\Lambda(\mu^{\prime},x^{\prime})

for a suitable Λ∈𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ)\Lambda\in\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}). We remark that composing context-free or in-context maps successively is possible under our architectural assumptions, since both context-free and in-context maps in 𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ)\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}) can represent the identity map. Therefore, composing multiple context-free MLPs to realize FF does not violate the in-context formulation. Moreover, the integration operation in ∫v⊤∘F∘Q​d​(μ−μ′)\int v^{\top}\circ F\circ Q\,d(\mu-\mu^{\prime}) can be implemented by a single in-context layer. See Appendix F for the complete proof.

5 Discussion

We introduced a new gradient-descent type in-context mapping. This consists of an attention mechanism interpreted as a nonexpansive update of the query driven by a context-dependent potential. We then studied its approximation properties in an abstract setting where the context is modeled as a probability measure, and its Lipschitz continuity with respect to the context is controlled in the Wasserstein-11 metric. In particular, we established a universal approximation theorem for Lipschitz-continuous in-context Transformers built from these Lipschitz primitives. Beyond existence, the proof is constructive: a Restricted Stone-Weierstrass argument reduces density to the ability to build minimax compositions of elementary Lipschitz primitives, and, in the measure-theoretic setting, these primitives arise naturally from Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality. This perspective yields concrete guidance for the design of Lipschitz-preserving in-context architectures and highlights two structural properties that drive universality in our approach: closure under lattice-type operations (Lemma 11) and the ability to represent the identity map.

Several directions are required to bridge the gap between this abstract universality result and practical, certifiable architectures. First, the step size ηℓ\eta_{\ell} in our in-context attention layers depends on the layerwise input domain Ωℓ\Omega_{\ell}. This input domain is, in general, difficult to estimate precisely. Second, while context-free Lipschitz control can be enforced by spectral-norm constraints, the corresponding bound for in-context attention is expressed through a supremum quantity that may be difficult to estimate or certify in practice. A natural next step is therefore to design alternative Lipschitz in-context mappings whose Lipschitz constants admit explicit, tractable upper bounds while preserving the algebraic properties used in the density proof. Since our argument is modular, we expect the same proof strategy to transfer to other in-context mechanisms that retain (i) lattice-type closure and (ii) identity representability.

Finally, our analysis focuses on scalar-valued targets. Extending universality to vector-valued outputs is nontrivial even in the context-free 11-Lipschitz setting, and will likely require new approximation mechanisms beyond the scalar proof strategy. A key obstruction is that the pointwise lattice structure (closure under max\max and min\min) that underpins the Restricted Stone-Weierstrass argument in the scalar case does not extend canonically to vector-valued mappings, where no natural total order is available. Establishing such extensions would enable a more comprehensive approximation theory for Lipschitz Transformers and further clarify which Lipschitz-preserving design choices are most compatible with practice.

=𝔼μx​[(A​Y−m⁡(x))​(A​Y)⊤]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{x}}\bigl[(AY-m(x))(AY)^{\top}\bigr]
=𝔼μx​[(A​Y−m⁡(x))​(A​Y−m⁡(x))⊤]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{x}}\bigl[(AY-m(x))(AY-m(x))^{\top}\bigr]
=Covμx​[A​Y],\displaystyle=\mathrm{Cov}_{\mu_{x}}[AY],

where

m⁡(x):=∫e⟨x,A​y⟩∫e⟨x,A​z⟩​𝑑μ​(z)​A​y​𝑑μ​(y)=𝔼μx​[A​Y],m(x):=\int\frac{e^{\langle x,Ay\rangle}}{\int e^{\langle x,Az\rangle}\,d\mu(z)}Ay\,d\mu(y)=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{x}}[AY],

≤supy∈Ω‖A​y‖22.\displaystyle\leq\sup_{y\in\Omega}\|Ay\|_{2}^{2}.

(2) Fix x∈Ωx\in\Omega. Define

and moreover

|1Zx​(μ)−1Zx​(ν)|≤e2​B​|Zx​(μ)−Zx​(ν)|,\Bigl|\frac{1}{Z_{x}(\mu)}-\frac{1}{Z_{x}(\nu)}\Bigr|\leq e^{2B}|Z_{x}(\mu)-Z_{x}(\nu)|,

we obtain

‖Nx​(μ)Zx​(μ)−Nx​(ν)Zx​(ν)‖2≤C​W1​(μ,ν),\Bigl\|\frac{N_{x}(\mu)}{Z_{x}(\mu)}-\frac{N_{x}(\nu)}{Z_{x}(\nu)}\Bigr\|_{2}\leq C\,W_{1}(\mu,\nu),

Appendix B Proof of Lemma 9

The proof follows from a slight modification of (Anil et al., 2019, Lemma 1), adapted to functions of two variables with possibly different Lipschitz constants.

Let g∈𝒞1,C​(U×X,ℝ)g\in\mathcal{C}_{1,C}(U\times X,\mathbb{R}) and let ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1). Since U×XU\times X is compact and gg is continuous, we have

‖g‖∞:=sup(u,x)∈U×X|g⁡(x,u)|<∞.\|g\|_{\infty}:=\sup_{(u,x)\in U\times X}|g(x,u)|<\infty.

Define

gε:=(1−ε2​(1+‖g‖∞))​g.g_{\varepsilon}:=\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2(1+\|g\|_{\infty})}\right)g.

Then

|gε​(u,x)−g⁡(u,x)|≤ε/2for all ​(u,x)∈U×X,|g_{\varepsilon}(u,x)-g(u,x)|\leq\varepsilon/2\qquad\text{for all }(u,x)\in U\times X,

and gε∈𝒞1,C​(U×X,ℝ)g_{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{C}_{1,C}(U\times X,\mathbb{R}). Thus, it suffices to approximate gεg_{\varepsilon} within accuracy ε/2\varepsilon/2.

Fix (u,x)∈U×X(u,x)\in U\times X. For each (v,y)∈U×X(v,y)\in U\times X, by the separation property (B) of LL, there exists a function f(v,y)∈Lf_{(v,y)}\in L such that

f(v,y)​(u,x)=gε​(u,x),f(v,y)​(v,y)=gε​(v,y).f_{(v,y)}(u,x)=g_{\varepsilon}(u,x),\qquad f_{(v,y)}(v,y)=g_{\varepsilon}(v,y).

Indeed, since x↦gε​(u,x)x\mapsto g_{\varepsilon}(u,x) is (1−ε2​(1+‖g‖∞))\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2(1+\|g\|_{\infty})}\right)-Lipschitz and u↦gε​(u,x)u\mapsto g_{\varepsilon}(u,x) is C⁡(1−ε2​(1+‖g‖∞))C\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2(1+\|g\|_{\infty})}\right)-Lipschitz, we have

|gε​(u,x)−gε​(v,y)|\displaystyle|g_{\varepsilon}(u,x)-g_{\varepsilon}(v,y)| ≤(1−ε2​(1+‖g‖∞))​(dX​(x,y)+C​dU​(u,v))\displaystyle\leq\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2(1+\|g\|_{\infty})}\right)\bigl(d_{X}(x,y)+C\,d_{U}(u,v)\bigr)
<dX​(x,y)+C​dU​(u,v),\displaystyle<d_{X}(x,y)+C\,d_{U}(u,v),

which allows us to apply condition (B).

Define the open set

V(v,y):={(w,z)∈U×X|f(v,y)​(w,z)<gε​(w,z)+ε/2}.V_{(v,y)}:=\bigl\{(w,z)\in U\times X\;\big|\;f_{(v,y)}(w,z)<g_{\varepsilon}(w,z)+\varepsilon/2\bigr\}.

Then V(v,y)V_{(v,y)} is open and contains both (u,x)(u,x) and (v,y)(v,y). Hence, the family {V(v,y)}(v,y)∈U×X\{V_{(v,y)}\}_{(v,y)\in U\times X} forms an open cover of U×XU\times X. By compactness, there exists a finite subcover {V(v1,y1),…,V(vn,yn)}\{V_{(v_{1},y_{1})},\ldots,V_{(v_{n},y_{n})}\}.

Define

F(u,x):=min⁡{f(v1,y1),…,f(vn,yn)}.F_{(u,x)}:=\min\bigl\{f_{(v_{1},y_{1})},\ldots,f_{(v_{n},y_{n})}\bigr\}.

Since LL is a lattice by assumption (A), we have F(u,x)∈LF_{(u,x)}\in L. Moreover,

F(u,x)​(u,x)=gε​(u,x),F(u,x)​(w,z)<gε​(w,z)+ε/2for all ​(w,z)∈U×X.F_{(u,x)}(u,x)=g_{\varepsilon}(u,x),\qquad F_{(u,x)}(w,z)<g_{\varepsilon}(w,z)+\varepsilon/2\quad\text{for all }(w,z)\in U\times X.

Next, define

U(u,x):={(w,z)∈U×X|F(u,x)​(w,z)>gε​(w,z)−ε/2}.U_{(u,x)}:=\bigl\{(w,z)\in U\times X\;\big|\;F_{(u,x)}(w,z)>g_{\varepsilon}(w,z)-\varepsilon/2\bigr\}.

Then U(u,x)U_{(u,x)} is an open neighborhood of (u,x)(u,x). The collection {U(u,x)}(u,x)∈U×X\{U_{(u,x)}\}_{(u,x)\in U\times X} forms an open cover of U×XU\times X, and hence admits a finite subcover {U(u1,x1),…,U(um,xm)}\{U_{(u_{1},x_{1})},\ldots,U_{(u_{m},x_{m})}\}.

Define

G:=max⁡{F(u1,x1),…,F(um,xm)}.G:=\max\bigl\{F_{(u_{1},x_{1})},\ldots,F_{(u_{m},x_{m})}\bigr\}.

Again, by the lattice property, G∈LG\in L. Furthermore, for all (w,z)∈U×X(w,z)\in U\times X, we have

gε​(w,z)−ε/2<G⁡(w,z)<gε​(w,z)+ε/2.g_{\varepsilon}(w,z)-\varepsilon/2<G(w,z)<g_{\varepsilon}(w,z)+\varepsilon/2.

Therefore,

‖gε−G‖∞<ε/2.\|g_{\varepsilon}-G\|_{\infty}<\varepsilon/2.

Thus, we conclude that LL is dense in 𝒞1,C​(U×X,ℝ)\mathcal{C}_{1,C}(U\times X,\mathbb{R}) with respect to the uniform norm. ∎

Appendix C Proof of Lemma 10

Let Λ∈𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ)\Lambda\in\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}). By definition, Λ\Lambda admits a representation of the form

Λ⁡(μ,x)\displaystyle\Lambda(\mu,x) =v⊤∘π2∘F¯ξL∘Γ¯θL∘⋯∘F¯ξ1∘Γ¯θ1∘Q¯(μ,x)\displaystyle=v^{\top}\circ\pi_{2}\circ\bar{F}_{\xi_{L}}\circ\bar{\Gamma}_{\theta_{L}}\circ\cdots\circ\bar{F}_{\xi_{1}}\circ\bar{\Gamma}_{\theta_{1}}\circ\bar{Q}(\mu,x)
=v⊤∘FξL∘ΓθL(μL)∘⋯∘Fξ1∘Γθ1(μ1)∘Q(x),\displaystyle=v^{\top}\circ F_{\xi_{L}}\circ\Gamma_{\theta_{L}}(\mu_{L})\circ\cdots\circ F_{\xi_{1}}\circ\Gamma_{\theta_{1}}(\mu_{1})\circ Q(x),

where the intermediate measures and features are defined recursively by

μ1\displaystyle\mu_{1} :=Q♯​μ,z1:=Q⁡(x),\displaystyle:=Q_{\sharp}\mu,\qquad z_{1}:=Q(x),
μℓ+1\displaystyle\mu_{\ell+1} :=(Fξℓ∘Γθℓ​(μℓ))♯​μℓ,zℓ+1:=Fξℓ∘Γθℓ​(μℓ)​(zℓ),\displaystyle:=(F_{\xi_{\ell}}\circ\Gamma_{\theta_{\ell}}(\mu_{\ell}))_{\sharp}\mu_{\ell},\qquad z_{\ell+1}:=F_{\xi_{\ell}}\circ\Gamma_{\theta_{\ell}}(\mu_{\ell})(z_{\ell}),

for ℓ=1,…,L−1\ell=1,\dots,L-1.

Let Λ,Λ′∈𝒢C​(𝒳,ℝ)\Lambda,\Lambda^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}_{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}) be given by

Λ⁡(μ,x)\displaystyle\Lambda(\mu,x) =v⊤∘FξL∘ΓθL(μL)∘⋯∘Fξ1∘Γθ1(μ1)∘Q(x),\displaystyle=v^{\top}\circ F_{\xi_{L}}\circ\Gamma_{\theta_{L}}(\mu_{L})\circ\cdots\circ F_{\xi_{1}}\circ\Gamma_{\theta_{1}}(\mu_{1})\circ Q(x),
Λ′​(μ,x)\displaystyle\Lambda^{\prime}(\mu,x) =v′⁣⊤∘FξL′∘ΓθL′(μL′)∘⋯∘Fξ1′∘Γθ1′(μ1′)∘Q′(x),\displaystyle=v^{\prime\top}\circ F_{\xi^{\prime}_{L}}\circ\Gamma_{\theta^{\prime}_{L}}(\mu^{\prime}_{L})\circ\cdots\circ F_{\xi^{\prime}_{1}}\circ\Gamma_{\theta^{\prime}_{1}}(\mu^{\prime}_{1})\circ Q^{\prime}(x),

with

Γθℓ∈𝒱h,Ωℓ,Ω~ℓ,Γθℓ′∈𝒱h′,Ωℓ′,Ω~ℓ′,Fξℓ∈ℰh,Ω~ℓ,Ωℓ+1,Fξℓ′∈ℰh′,Ω~ℓ′,Ωℓ+1′.\Gamma_{\theta_{\ell}}\in\mathcal{V}_{h,\Omega_{\ell},\tilde{\Omega}_{\ell}},\quad\Gamma_{\theta^{\prime}_{\ell}}\in\mathcal{V}_{h^{\prime},\Omega^{\prime}_{\ell},\tilde{\Omega}^{\prime}_{\ell}},\quad F_{\xi_{\ell}}\in\mathcal{E}_{h,\tilde{\Omega}_{\ell},\Omega_{\ell+1}},\quad F_{\xi^{\prime}_{\ell}}\in\mathcal{E}_{h^{\prime},\tilde{\Omega}^{\prime}_{\ell},\Omega^{\prime}_{\ell+1}}.

Without loss of generality, we may assume that both networks have the same depth, since identity mappings can be represented by attention and MLP layers.

We first concatenate the two networks in parallel:
